items.text: The 5-Step Decision Ladder: real shortlist, hard-constraint cut, weighted scoring, one cheap real test, decide-by date with a review step.
Instead of choosing between "decide fast" and "wait forever," run every real option through the same five-step sequence.
Separate what you are actually considering from what you are only curious about, and cap the real list at three or four options.
Screen out anything that fails a non-negotiable first - budget, family expectations, location, a minimum qualification, or a fixed timeline - before you let yourself get attached to it.
Most people carry two lists in their head at once: options they are actually taking real steps toward, and options they are merely curious about or someone else keeps mentioning.
Write down only what you have taken a real, concrete step toward in the last few months - applied, researched seriously, spoken to someone in the field, or started learning a related skill.
Cap it at three or four items.

blocks.heading: "What Career Should I Choose" Open Forever

items.text: Most people who stay stuck on this question for years are not lacking information.

Research on "overchoice" has repeatedly found that once a choice set grows past a handful of live options, decision confidence and satisfaction drop even as the options stay equally good on paper - more open tabs do not mean a clearer answer, they mean a heavier one.

Psychologist Herbert Simon's concept of satisficing - choosing the first option that clears your own bar instead of hunting for the mathematically best one - was later tested directly against maximizing by Barry Schwartz and colleagues, who found maximizers report lower decision satisfaction and more regret than satisficers, despite often ending up with objectively similar outcomes.

items.text: Whether the option you grabbed under pressure survives contact with a real constraint - money, family, or a fixed timeline - once you are already six months in.
Whether you actually compared it against your other real options, or just picked whichever one happened to come up first.
Whether the appeal was ever tested against the real day-to-day work, or only against the idea of the work.

blocks.heading: Mistakes People Make Trying to Decide

items.text: Treating a bigger shortlist as more thorough research.
Scoring appeal before applying hard constraints.

Sunk-cost reasoning treats time and money already spent as if they were still a reason to continue, when the only real question is which option is the better bet from today forward, regardless of what it cost to get here.
Setting an intention instead of a specific plan.
Testing your feelings about the option instead of the option itself.
